Raising rates will have one main effect. Raising prices.

Most of the drivers right now of inflation are in-elastic demand. Raising the cost of borrowing, will not deter that spend.

What it will do, is actually drive up the cost of all business, and worsen employment simultaneously. You can typically see a rise in prices (inflation) following a rate hike. Even when it's needed to combat regular elastic demand side inflation, it takes time to have a positive effect. If the main driver of the inflation is inelastic, or rate insensitive as much of the driving force right now is, hiking rates will actually increase inflation.

The AI boom doesn't care what rate it has to pay, it will pay it, and keep driving things up.

What's needed is a significant policy shift, to make room in the markets again for things society needs financing for (ex. building homes, productive revenue generating businesses)

title: Governments are mishandling the affordability crisis
text:
OP mentioned that inflation is confusing because people often don't realize that inflation is relative to their wages. I'm not denying that.

My issue with your criticism specifically was that you called out the example. It's like if someone had issue with Hitler, but their criticisms only focused on Hitler's choice of clothing.

"Boo Hitler! Not because of his ideology though, but because the collars he wore were too tight!" This is ridiculous because even if your criticism is valid, you are just criticizing the wrong thing.

    > That's not how the economy works.

    > yeah but it's not a great example, because actually wages aren't going up.

    > my point is that's a bad example because we couldn't say that that's true given that the cost od living has been out-pacing wage inflation for a long time.
All of these quotes have you fixating on the numbers. If you take only one thing from this entire reply, let it be this: *the example works regardless of the numbers used*. My whole point is that whether wages rise with inflation or not, the example's (not any surrounding exchange, just the example) only purpose was to illustrate that wages are relative to inflation. It did that.

To take this even further, and make it so even a bird-brain like myself can't possibly misunderstand, let's look at my previous example with the Nazis. Does my analogy stop working if I switch "Hiter" with "Stalin", or him with "bin Laden"?

"Boo Stalin! Not because of the Great Purge, but because of his funny mustache!"

See how the point being made remains exactly the same, regardless of whom you use to illustrate it? Please, please, please try to understand this.

And as this has now become a stress test for how thoroughly I want to humiliate myself through meaningless argument, let me also briefly address your argument on the data.

    > as for how real wages have changed overtime, you should be aware that it isn't a straight-forward measurment, and that it is an area of active political contestation.
Of course it's politically contested, but that doesn't mean we're just nowhere; absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. We have some statistics that can give us some good idea of wages relative to inflation, and the graphs I gave you were a very good start. Especially the one from FRED, where three different earnings metrics are supplied--at the very least this is an okay proxy for income.

    > there are ways you can slice it to make things look one way or another.
Yes, there are different ways to interpret the data. This is why I said that the affordability problem is real.

But this is not the claim you made. Your claim was much stronger, and much less defensible. You said that wages outpacing cost of living/inflation is unrealistic, and critically, that inflation had outpaced wages for "a long time."

This is just false. Inflation generally outpacing wages for "a long time" is just not a conclusion you can make based on the data. We can have more nuanced conversation about this, but here specifically I think you're trying to take your broad, conclusive, and incorrect claim, and equivocate it into a smaller, more defensible, but different claim.

text:
No, the point of the example was not to make any specific claim about wages or inflation. The point of the example was to illustrate that wages and inflation are relative. That's it.

If instead OP had said "if wages go up 500%, and prices go up 1,000%, everyone is worse off and got a 500% pay cut", then the main point being made would remain exactly the same. Again, this is because the exact numbers were never relevant, and the example was for explanation purposes.

Now apart from the fact that we are now 6 comments deep in the most pedantic thread I have ever had the displeasure of participating in (this is my fault too, to be fair), you also might be interested to know that cost of living/inflation has not outpaced wages for a "long time" as you so claim.

Here's a graph from the last 30 years, for example, showing earnings keeping up with inflation.

https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/?g=iuyN

Or maybe you'd just like to look at more recently, in which case, looking at just the past year, wages have still kept up.

https://usafacts.org/answers/are-wages-keeping-up-with-infla...

Or if your a low wage earner, those wages have especially kept up, outpacing inflation and even high wage earners by significant margin in recent years.

https://www.epi.org/publication/strong-wage-growth-for-low-w...

This is not to say that there is no affordability problem, but no matter what way you put it, your specific claim, that wages have not been outpaced by inflation "for a long time", is demonstrably false.

title: Ask HN: Why do people say "I built it" when we should say "Claude built it"?
text:
A lot of interesting perspectives. There is a lot of nuance, which I think is actually the fair approach.

If you ask Claude to “Build me a CRM application.” and then walk away for 9 hours, then you should say Claude built this. That’s giving the technology and the time we live in the credit it deserves. A lot people made that possible.

If you work with Claude to create something during your days, nights, and weekends, then you created it. No one has the right to tell you how to use the tools at your disposal. Just like an artist shouldn’t be told they didn’t create something by using Photoshop vs. using a piece of charcoal sourced from a fireplace on a piece of parchment.

If you have a shower thought for a particularly novel concept that no one has thought of and then use Claude to bring that concept to reality, then you absolutely get credit for the creation. Who gives a shit how it was coded. The only ones that will care how it was coded will be the jealous ones that didn’t think of the concept themselves.

Blaming AI is also nuanced as well. Just like blaming a company for layoffs vs. not blaming the CEO by name. Just like if AI deletes everything vs. why the hell did you run AI on production systems. If you’re well liked, then AI takes the blame, if not, then you’re getting shitcanned for being boneheaded enough to use AI anywhere near important data.

title: Do dentists know what they're doing?
text:
I feel for this guy, so much. I bounced around between dentists, and may have even encountered the guy on Wilshire. But despite night grinding, TMJ and stage 4-5 gum recession, I've found stability after a bunch of years and dentists that I told to go pound sand when they wanted to make substantial physical modifications to my teeth. One of the worst was in Santa Monica; his AI receptionist still calls me trying to book appointments so they can drill in my "overdue fillings". Garbage.

What worked for me: Spider silk floss - It's thicker and somehow smoother than the "waxed" PFOS crud. Does a great job of getting stuff out of the pockets between teeth. LIVFRESH toothpaste - Better than any other toothpaste despite having no abrasives. Expensive as hell but you do only need a tiny amount. Just get used to putting water on your toothbrush first, it somehow evaporates on contact. Therasol mouthwash - Does this weird thing that wraps up any leftover food bits in your mouth into a gel you can easily spit out. Lasts for hours. Absolutely nothing like listerine or any other mouthwash I've ever tried.

Also use a tongue scraper, ultrasonic night-guard cleaner (the $20 ones work just fine) and occasionally use a Proclaim water flosser. The former are amazingly valuable, the latter... is fine I guess. It's not a substitute for real flossing. Hope this helps someone.

title: The United Kingdom generates less electricity per person than in the 1970s
text:
You're not wrong, but you are mostly arguing against an exaggerated version of what I have said (focus steel production, ignoring qualifiers like 'moderate', 'since the 90s', 'public private' vs your 'state ownership' (which I only applied to infrastructure)).

Industrial policy should be measured by how industry delivers for the goals of the population - cleaner greener infrastructure, high-quality housing, and high wages. By that standard, Britain has had worse industrial policy than its comparable neighbours. Rather than pretending that this isn't the case, we should ask why. Britain led the neoliberal project since 1979 and applied its teachings deeply. What does it have to show for it?

> If an industry is uncompetitive, public ownership does not magically make it productive

Shrewd investments make productivity, and the public is generally incentivised to make these investments unlike owners - who can simply move the money to low-cost countries. Limited public ownership and the other structures I mentioned help to ensure that the profits are reinvested back into domestic industry. If you sell to the highest bidder, you can be certain that the profits will be taken overseas. Of course, the devil is in the detail, and this may be a sound decision (e.g. if you had other more critical industries in need of capital). But since these decisions are made by private owners, and not by the public, such cases are exceedingly rare.

> A competitive manufacturing sector is not primarily the result of protectionism. It depends on ..

You then list all the things I claimed the other states have intervened more heavily in, and which British neoliberal doctrine insists on leaving to the market.

Limited strategic protectionism for emerging industries has a long history in economics and left-wing political economy. It was practiced liberally in all ascendant industrial powers - China, US, Germany, and of course the UK. Only in the anglosphere and only since Thatcher and Reagan era propaganda have such policies come to be viewed with suspicion. Since the 70s, the Nordic countries have embraced it too. Norway protected its oil and gas industries, Sweden and Finland protected telecommunications (Nokia, Ericsson), Denmark protected its offshore wind. In these cases, state ownership (of the customers) was indeed the key mechanism. The list is long and many of those defining features of the modern sophisticated Nordic economies are the consequence of protectionism.

> But it does not establish that this is the primary reason for their higher living standards

If not from industry, then where does the Wealth of Nations come? If banking and finance service only foreign industry, and domestic real estate, what good are they for the development of the country? On these subjects, there has been much ink spilled.

I for one confidently believe that it is no coincidence that UK has experienced less growth and improvement of living standards, while its industrial base declined more rapidly. To find a counterexample you would have to go as far as Italy - a country with extreme political corruption during the period in question.

> or that their manufacturing success was primarily caused by the policies you advocate

No it doesn't, but I hope that at it least has led you to consider the possibility.

title: What I self-host
text:
I self host (I have a large overlap with the services in TFA), and love it. I will never go back and think that more people should self host (or at least...join small groups of people who designate one person to manage it for a small number of people).

And believing that the current AI economy might have a period of rapid devaluation in the near future is pretty reasonable. But, much like the original .com bubble, the idea that AI as a technology will not survive and thrive through such a pop, and become an ever more important part of our future, is a belief that I can't comprehend. Anthropic and OpenAI very well may go belly up. AI as a technology isn't going anywhere.

And as much as I'd like to believe that more people may self host more things in the future, self hosting will never, even if it was adopted by literally everyone, become as big a deal as AI, even if AI hit a wall tomorrow and didn't get any better than the current frontier models.
